items.title: Biological passports
items.claim: WADA introduced the Athlete Biological Passport in 2009 to detect doping. What does it primarily monitor?

options.text: Longitudinal changes in biomarkers (e.g. haematological) that suggest manipulation, even without a positive substance test

items.reveal:
The passport tracks haematological, steroidal and (more recently) endocrine markers across an athlete's career. Significant deviations can trigger sanctions even without finding the substance itself.

The approach has produced sanctions where direct testing failed.
items.why: Indirect, statistical evidence has become a major tool in anti-doping enforcement.

items.title: CTE and contact sports
items.claim: Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative condition linked to repeated head impacts. What is true about diagnosis?

options.text: It is reliably diagnosed in life
Definitive diagnosis is currently only possible at post-mortem
It can be diagnosed by a single blood test

items.reveal:
Mez et al. (2017, JAMA) reported CTE pathology in 110 of 111 deceased NFL players whose brains were examined. The sample was self-selected, but the proportion is striking.

In-life diagnostic biomarkers are an active research area.
items.why: Sport policy operates under uncertainty when the condition cannot be confirmed in living athletes.

items.title: First modern Olympics
items.claim: Approximately how many athletes competed at the first modern Olympics in Athens 1896?
items.reveal:
Sources vary from around 241 to 280 athletes from roughly 14 nations.

Women first competed at Paris 1900 (in tennis, golf and a few other sports).
items.why: The scale of contemporary Olympics is not built in; it grew from a modest revival.
